newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Denktash blames EU for "Greek tragedy" in Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Denktash blames EU for "Greek tragedy" in Cyprus.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash accused the European Union on Thursday of turning Cyprus unity talks into a "Greek tragedy."
The 73-year-old Denktash warned he would pull out of the talks unless Brussels freezes its decision to start EU entry talks with the Greek Cypriot government.

"The European Union is the stumbling block. If the EU...treats the Greek Cypriots as Cyprus then what's the use of talking?" he said after the fourth day of talks with Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides and U.N. mediator Diego Cordovez.
"This is the last round until the EU decides," he told reporters in Montreux following the meeting in the nearby village of Glion.
Denktash said he would stay at the negotiating table in Glion until the end of the deadlocked talks on Friday.

But he added: "We will have to wait to see whether the EU will regard us as an existing factor for Cyprus or continue to disregard us. It is a very big tragedy the EU has committed while the talks were going on."
"It is a Greek tragedy."
On Thursday, the U.N. struggled to revive momentum.

Officials said Cordovez met both Clerides and Denktash to discuss the text of a possible U.N. statement acceptable to both sides on extending the talks over the status of the eastern Mediterranean island.
Denktash said negotiations were continuing on the text.

Diplomats said Cordovez, British ambassador David Hannay and the U.S. and EU envoys tried unsuccessfully to persuade Denktash to drop his opposition. One said Cordovez told him that he would be considered as the "intransigent" side if he did not do so.
Denktash said: "They blame my side all the way because we don`t accept the Greek Cypriots as our government. We are treated as the guilty side. But we are used to it."
The talks are the second round following July's inconclusive start in New York. Prior to this session, Turkish Cypriots had ruled out signing a joint document.

On Wednesday Denktash refused to sign a new, amended U.N. proposal until the EU shelves plans for entry talks with the internationally-recognised Greek Cypriot government early next year, saying Cordovez tabled it despite his objection.

The document dealt with the drafting of a new constitution and the issues of sovereignty, territory, refugees, security and guarantor states that have for decades blocked efforts to reunite Cyprus in a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Officials said Clerides found it broadly acceptable but wanted guarantees that a paragraph for the two sides to refrain from action that may damage the process did not refer to EU process.
Denktash said: "I say that if the EU treats the Greek Cypriots as its interlocutor I will not talk. Mr Clerides now says that if the EU delays, he will not talk."
"The EU has succeeded in creating the best impasse ever in the Cyprus problem. They can be congratulated."
Under the proposed procedure, the pair was to study the documents and respond by the end of 1997 and start real talks after the Greek Cypriot presidential election in February.
The island has been divided since 1974 when Turkey occupied its north in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.

The amended U.N. document was the third tabled since the start of the first round of talks in New York by Cordovez, who is trying to draw out a compromise by concocting working papers with different options while trying to keep the talks going.
But it is unclear whether Cordovez will be able to coax Clerides, 78, and Denktash into open ground from positions which both have held unchanged for more than 20 years.
